ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection causing fever, sweats, arthralgia and hepatosplenomegaly. Diagnosis relies on serology and culture; treatment combines doxycycline with an aminoglycoside.

sections.p: Brucellosis is a systemic bacterial infection transmitted from animals (usually via unpasteurised dairy or occupational exposure). Diagnosis requires compatible clinical syndrome plus a positive serologic test (standard agglutination titre ≥1:160) or isolation of Brucella from blood, bone marrow or tissue.
b: Blood culture is definitive but low yield
PCR can be used when labs are limited

t.b: Does the patient have a significant antibody titre? A titre ≥1:160 (or four‑fold rise) supports active infection.
Is Brucella grown? Positive culture confirms diagnosis; if unavailable, rely on serology and clinical picture.
Detects bacterial DNA; useful when culture is negative or delayed, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Acute brucellosis lasts ≤2 months, sub‑acute 2–6 months, chronic >6 months. Severity is graded by organ involvement: uncomplicated (fever, arthralgia), focal (osteomyelitis, endocarditis, neuro‑brucellosis).
b: Chronic disease may mimic rheumatologic disorders

sections.p: Brucella species are gram‑negative coccobacilli. The most common human species are B. melitensis (goats/sheep), B. abortus (cattle), B. suis (pigs). Transmission is usually occupational (farmers, veterinarians) or through unpasteurised dairy.
b: B. melitensis – most virulent, common in Mediterranean and Middle East

sections.p: Patients develop intermittent fever, night sweats, malaise, arthralgia and often hepatosplenomegaly. Osteoarticular involvement (sacroiliitis, spondylitis) is common; neuro‑brucellosis and endocarditis are serious complications.
Beyond microbiology, routine labs show mild anemia, leukopenia or lymphocytosis, and elevated transaminases. Imaging is guided by focal symptoms.

t.b: Is there anemia or lymphocytosis? Suggests chronic infection; normal counts do not exclude disease.
Are transaminases elevated? Mild rise supports systemic infection; severe rise prompts evaluation for hepatic involvement.
Is there sacroiliitis or spondylitis? Positive findings indicate focal disease requiring longer therapy.

sections.p: Focal disease can be life‑threatening. Endocarditis, neuro‑brucellosis, and spondylodiscitis carry high morbidity and mortality if untreated.
b: New cardiac murmur or neurologic deficit
Severe back pain with neurologic signs

sections.p: First‑line therapy combines doxycycline (bacteriostatic, intracellular penetration) with an aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin) for synergy. Duration is 6 weeks for uncomplicated disease, longer for focal involvement. Supportive care includes antipyretics and physiotherapy for joint pain.
b: If aminoglycoside unavailable, use rifampicin with doxycycline

sections.p: Repeat serology at 6 weeks to confirm falling titres; monitor for relapse. Prevention focuses on animal‑health measures, pasteurisation of dairy, and protective equipment for high‑risk workers.
b: Educate farmers on safe animal handling

sections.p: Brucellosis mimics other febrile illnesses with arthralgia and organomegaly.
b: Typhoid fever – similar fever pattern but no occupational animal exposure
Tuberculosis – chronic fever, weight loss, but usually pulmonary focus
Malaria – intermittent fever, but peripheral smear differentiates
Rheumatic fever – joint pain, but lacks hepatosplenomegaly

sections.p: Serology may be negative early or in chronic disease; cultures are often false‑negative; liver enzymes can be normal despite organ involvement.
b: Aminoglycoside toxicity can mask renal dysfunction if not monitored

whenToSeekHelp: New cardiac murmur, neurologic deficits, persistent fever despite therapy, severe back pain with neurologic signs

faq.a: It penetrates macrophages where Brucella hides, providing intracellular activity.

faq.q: Can brucellosis be cured without antibiotics?
faq.a: No; untreated infection often becomes chronic and may cause organ damage.

faq.q: Is a negative blood culture enough to rule out disease?
faq.a: No; cultures are low‑yield. Serology and clinical context are essential.
